utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, is this Mr. Kristo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, this is Mr. Kristo. And the next one is Mr. Miketa.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone to the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is Mr. Kristo, and the next witness will be Mr. Miketa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's see if we can get through both of them this morning. Yes. Would you take -- let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kristo. Thank you for coming here. I'm first going to ask you to state your full name for the record, as well as the date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: My name is Slavko Kristo. I was born on 1 April 1952 in Poculica, Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your ethnic background is Croatian; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is your religion?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I am an economist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where do you work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I am a branch manager of the Herzegovina Bank from Mostar, in branch management Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where did you complete -- where did you graduate from high school?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I finished high school in Travnik and graduated from the school of economics in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, I got married in 1982. I have a daughter Josipa born in 1983 and a son born in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I am a member -- I have been a member of HDZ since 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you hold any position in the party?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I am a member of the municipal board. This is since June 2000, that is, the new elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You have siblings?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, a brother lives in Vitez with my mother, and two other siblings work in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Originally, your family comes from Poculica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: My family was expelled, that is, my mother, my sister and my brother, and I had left Poculica sometime ago and I have lived in Vitez since 1982 in an apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We'll go back to that but now that we mention Poculica, perhaps to -- we need to mention something that I don't think anyone else has mentioned before. Is there a mosque in Poculica?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, and it is right next to my family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, have you had an opportunity to see this mosque immediately following -- after the Washington Accords in 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I saw it about 15 days ago because I was going on business in -- to Zenica, and I passed by there because the road takes me past there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is the mosque still there undamaged, intact as before the war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That is correct. It is still there intact like other mosques in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not bother to ask the witness about paragraph 2.1 and 2.2 since it was repeated many times. If there is a question on cross, I will not object and perhaps only a question on paragraph 2.3 and then further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Kristo, I'm going to shorten my examination because we are pressed for time. I am going to go directly to the events of late 1992 and early 1993. Did, during that period, some HVO unit arrive there which was not a local one?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. In late 1992 early 1993, there were units from Herzegovina there. There was Bruno Busic and Ludwig Pavlovic units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was there an increased number of incidents in the area during that time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In late 1992 and early 1993, one could feel that it was an unusual situation, that it was a lot more chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that this development coincides with the influx of refugees, in other words, were refugees still coming in that late?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. My brother and sisters are refugees from Vlasic. After the fall of Jajce, the influx of refugees from Jajce and Kotor Varos increased as well as Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your estimate, did all this contribute to this unrestful situation in town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. This has all contributed to the sense of insecurity in town and the lack of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether one of these two units that you mentioned, did one of these two units stay in the Vitez area for a longer period of time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. The Bruno Busic unit left some time in late 1992, early 1993, while members of the Ludwig Pavlovic stayed until the end of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, where did you live in 1993 on the eve of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Since 1983, I have been living in the so-called yellow building right next to the marketplace, about 200 metres from the parking structure which separates the old Vitez from the rest of the town. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that your building, when the general conflict broke out between the HVO and the ABiH, was at the line of separation between the two parties, that is, between the Mahala part and the new Vitez part of town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. We had trenches on each side of the building, and the physical obstacle between the two warring parties were literally those garages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How many tenants were there in your building before the war or let's say how many units?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There were 50 units all together. There were two entryways with 25 units each.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the -- could you tell us what was the ethnic break down of the tenants in the building?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I could give you individual names, but I would say that 45 per cent each of the Muslims and Croats and about 10 per cent of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So Croats and Muslims comprised 90 per cent and the rest were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Perhaps 80 per cent. I could go name by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no need for that. The tenants organised themselves, given the lack of law and order?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In order to protect ourselves, in other words, in order to protect our families, and I'm talking only about my entrance, we tried to take stock of the new situation and to work out some kind of protection. This is why we organised duties at the entrance of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who took part in these guard duties?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In my entryway, there were about 12 Croats involved, 3 Serbs and no Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why the Muslims living in the building did not participant in this?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: This was offered to them but they did not have any interest to be with us, and some of them were spending nights outside of the building, most probably in Stari Vitez, in old Vitez, with their relatives. And I don't know what they did there but it is -- it needs to be pointed out that their families were still living there. In other words, I was in charge of protecting their families and they were probably protecting someone else's families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss this with other tenants so that these duties would be spread out evenly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There was no time for big discussions, because these duties, these guard duties, went on for only about ten days, from, let's say, the 2nd of April until the outbreak of hostilities. But let me add one thing which I believe is important. I moved into the building about five years after it was built, but my neighbour, Mr. Djukic, was very surprised that Mr. Djukic, who was also an educated man who was stating that he was for equality and everything and that he was not involved in this with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you started these guard duties only about ten days before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was there a special reason for it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. It was just a situation in town and general feeling of insecurity about our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a Mr. Djukic.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. Mr. Djukic, Nusret Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you also mentioned another man.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric. He was an ethnic Serb from the village of Poculica, in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where in the building was your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: My apartment was in the fourth floor at the end of the building, to the right-hand side. It was the last apartment on the fourth floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, did you have a view of downtown from there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What did you notice in early April in the area of the soccer stadium?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: We noticed trench-digging by Muslims, which concerned us even more, because we didn't even discuss trench-digging on our side in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that trenches were dug on both sides of the road connecting the bus station with the old Vitez, in other words, the road feeding into the main road?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct, because I used that road to go to work until the 15th of April. But I have to mention that there were not any incidents, but I noticed the trenches and I saw that they were facing the town, that is, my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If we were to show you the map of this town, you would be able to point that position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No problem. I can show it to you any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that in those days leading up to the conflict, you were still going to work. When did you last go to work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: On the 15th of April. And I have to say that I did not notice anything unusual. I was to go to work on the 16th, because I left my briefcase, my calculator, and some other items in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On 16 April 1993, in the morning, what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I was on guard duty. In other words, it was my -- my duty was between 2.00 and 4.00 a.m. I was very tired and I had just fallen asleep. I was asleep for an hour and then I was awakened by shooting. I was surprised. And bullets were flying all around to the building and everywhere. I ran down to the duty post. Others joined me there. We organised a little bit and then the military police arrived. No, the civilian police took me in front of the building of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of questions. On the night of the 15th to 16th, or on the evening of the 15th, were you advised, warned, that the next morning there could be a war?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Most of the population of Vitez, people that I have spoken with, were unaware of anything like that, and I vouch for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, we haven't addressed that topic very much. Do you know whether a general alert was sounded that morning?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I never heard any sirens. My building has a well-built basement which could be used as shelter, and we all could go there, and we did go there during the air raids of the JNA against the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on that critical morning on the 16th of April, did you ever go down into the shelter?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, after I got up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that during the day the civilian police summoned you and --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Not summoned me. They arrived here and we were escorted by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they came for you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Very early in the morning. That could have been 8.00, 8.30 in the morning when they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. That means it was early. And what kind of task did you receive in front of the police building, and from whom?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: At that moment people were gathering in front of the police building, that is, the able-bodied men, the militarily fit men. And about 45 minutes to maybe up to 70 minutes after I arrived there -- and there was confusion at first -- then Mr. Mirko Samija, the chief of the MUP, who also is an economist and who is also from that area, from Poculica, a place called Gola Kosa, so I've known him for years, he said that these people who arrived there without any training, without any uniforms, without any weapons, that I should -- who at that time I had some -- a modicum of knowledge about weapons, that I should show them how to use weapons, how to cock it, how to discharge it. And then with that short training, people were sent out to the line. And that took no more than about 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in that location there were military conscripts who had a duty, who were assigned to the civilian police and who had a duty to report there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I'm not aware of their assignments, but it was just plain gathering of people, collecting of people. There were people who had no assignments. These were not reserve police officers, those who would have known the system. So it was not the reserve police. These people were assigned to various specialties. One would go to some kind of exercise, another one was assigned to the civilian defence. So these were not reserve policemen; these were just general conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, I would like you to be very concise. From what you have just said, can we conclude that these people were summoned there, in fact, that the civilian police had brought them there regardless of their original wartime assignments?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in this confusion and in this speed with which things were happening, was this what was going on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So after this brief training, were you given a special assignment, a special defensive task?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: On the fourth day, I was sent to the Krtina-Mahala line which was above the line of Santici, Barin Gaj, Sljivcica and Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where were you until that time before you were sent to Barin Gaj?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Those three nights I had spent on the line at Pavlovica Kuce facing Stari Grad, that is old Vitez. Those were the nights of the 17th, 18th and 19th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am just waiting for the transcript. Was that part of the front line which was the part of the general line of separation of Mahala and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, because a formal line did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the place where you were for those three days, was there civilian police present?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the positions around you, would you be -- were you able to also see some other HVO units which you recognised?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you first: Who assigned you to that location at Krtina-Mahala above Buhine Kuce on that fourth day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I went there with the police and there, I -- the commander of this line became my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did he then tell you what your assignment was to be?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: It was interesting that at that time, this is -- this would be 21st and 22nd, I still did not know with whom I was. I was just sent to this trench, and only later they told me that I was a member of the Vitez Brigade of such and such battalion, such and such company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the situation when you arrived at the positions at Krtina-Mahala?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: You could still feel that the line was being fortified, that the trenches were being dug, the situation with weapons were very poor. I only had a weapon when I was on duty. I would leave it to the next person who would come to duty. I would go to the position where I would rest, and if there were -- there was to be an attack at that time, all I could do was throw rocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were trenches dug at the time when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: One part had been dug, one part was being dug, and I personally dug my own part of the trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Concerning the digging, I think you already answered part of that, you dug your own trench?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there any work platoons coming to dig?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: In addition to the soldiers who were at the front line, part of the trenches was dug by the local population, that is, inhabitants of that area. And only two nights, members of the work platoons arrived, once 8, once 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These were members of the work platoon brought in by the civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: They were brought in by someone, I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And during those days and -- or later, did you see people who had been brought to dig escorted by the military police?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear whether at a location where you were, detainees from the cinema theatre or other facilities where detainees were kept were brought there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I heard people say that they were brought to other parts of the front line, but they never came to where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the line then?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: About 100 days. Until I was wounded on the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the transcript now, it hasn't noted something so I'm going to ask you about that again. You said that on two occasions, you had organised work platoons that came through the civil defence. What was the ethnic composition of these work platoons?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: They were Romany.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were wounded, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I was taken to a make-shift clinic of the medical centre of Vitez. After a brief intervention, because they were not in a position to stop the bleeding, after four or five minutes, I proceeded to the hospital in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever return to the front line after that wounding?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't at the front line after that. After being treated in Nova Bila, I returned again to this make-shift medical centre, sort of like an in-patient clinic, and after the cease-fire was signed, I was treated in the Republic of Croatia when it became possible to travel there by regular bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you never returned to the front line again?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Apropos after the Washington Agreements, that is to say, April 1994 when you were in Croatia in hospital, did you see Muslims there at the time who were treated as patients at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Absolutely. Yes. That is quite correct. I saw Muslims who were wounded too. I don't know whether they were only members of the BH army, but probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you think that among the people you saw in hospital, there were civilians and members of the BH army who were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, and possibly Muslims who were members of other units in Posavina, Orasje who were together with the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were mobilised on the 16th in the civilian police, did your family stay in your apartment? Did they continue to live there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: On the third day or rather on the second day, to be precise, on the 18th in the evening, my family and most of the families from the yellow building, due to the general insecurity that prevailed, moved away. Only four or five tenants remained. This old woman whom no one could convince, and some old sisters -- I don't know -- this was on the side --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Facing town?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, facing town. While the other part of the building that was facing Stari Vitez that was being hit directly, there was really no one left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Where did you put your family up?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: At my father-in-law's place in Mosunj, an area that was safer, speaking very conditionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, while you were a soldier, did you ever take part in any offensive military action?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Because we never received orders at the front line that we should go out and conquer. It's not only that we did not receive such orders we could not have. There were shortages in terms of materiel, manpower and, as I said, Barin Gaj, Sljivcica, Sivrino Selo, that is where we were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: After it became obvious that you were a member of the Viteska Brigade, who were your first commanders whom you remember by name and surname?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Perica Miskovic and after him Josip Plavcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is Perica Miskovic still alive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, both are dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did both of them get killed?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During this approximately 100 days that you were at the front line. Yes, I'm going a bit too fast, yes. These approximately 100 days that you were at the front line, do you have any idea of how many of your men were killed during these approximately 100 days?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Nineteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Over 30, and all of this at the trenches, at the front line, snipers, front line, coming to and going from the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the war, you were granted 40 per cent disability?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I receive that kind of pension until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certificates were discussed extensively here, according to the rules passed by the federation. I'm not going to tire anybody with this, but just one question, is it true that the terms and conditions for granting these certificates were applied very liberally?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Living proof of this is the fact that my mother, my father-in-law and his wife who were quite old receive them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you are talking about your mother, Ljubica Kristo, born in 1920?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your father-in-law Dragutin Gudelj born in 1931?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: His wife, Kata, born 1930?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That means that you know that they received certificates and that they were listed there, although they were not members of the defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know why all of this turned out the way it did?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There were lists that involved direct or indirect participation. However, after that, a quota was set and people went around the village and said, "Let us use this quota that the HVO is entitled to and the quota that the army is entitled to," so that this total level could be met at a lower threshold.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir: The Muslims also applied these rules in an equally liberal fashion, is that right, very extensively?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Ultimately, all of these entitlements had to be paid from the same budget; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Federation budget?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you personally get some kind of paper?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I used part of this entitlement for buying the apartment on which I had a tenant's lease.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Others did not have that possibility. Privatisation funds are being established now, and perhaps then they will be able to use some of these shares.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that's what you're all hoping for; is that right? And one more question, perhaps, to take advantage of the fact that you are present here. You've known Mario Cerkez from before; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I know him personally. I've known him since 1978, ever since I arrived in Vitezit, although I would see him every now and then before that. But he finished a different kind of schooling. He lived in a different part of the municipality. So I knew him indirectly before, but actively I've known him since 1978, since I came to work in Vitezit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice any inclination on the part of Mario Cerkez to quarrel with other people, to be aggressive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. I wish all people were like Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions. I would like to thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kordic Defence has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been giving us a number of answers to Mr. Kovacic's questions about the distribution of money in both the Croat and the Muslims interests. Have you brought any documents to support what you say about the purpose of these certificates and what happened on the Muslim side as well as on the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I do not have a document. I could have brought my own document, but I did not take part in these activities. I am indirectly aware of this, since I work in a bank that will establish privatisation funds. So I will be in a position to have these papers in about two months' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just looking at these documents very quickly. We'll just have a look at them. 1232.1, please. This document is dated the 5th of October, signed by Mr. Cerkez, and it certifies that you have been a member of the Vitez Brigade since the 18th of April of 1993 and "he joined our unit as an active member and was wounded on the 26th of July," the document issued for regulating medical treatment. Have you ever seen that document before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just leave that one there and we'll look at another document, please, which is 1457.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Leave the first one available for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document is dated a little later, 14th of October, 1994, and comes from Mario Cerkez. And it confirms that you became a member of the Viteska Brigade on the 16th of April, 1993, and were wounded on the 26th of July. It sets out the circumstances of your being wounded. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. I have this document in my own medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Just one or two questions on these; that's all. The first document we looked at says --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- you joined as an active member. Does that indicate that you were formerly a reserve member?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I do not agree with this statement saying that I actively took part. I'm talking about D48028.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we're looking at the first document I showed you. That's the one, yes.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. 94 -- I actively took part, but not as an active member.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. Just one small point. There will be probably a long discussion on that term. It's simply a wrong translation. We checked it. It's not very precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which term?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The term in the Croatian text we have, "When he was actively included," and in the English text we have, "As an active member." "Actively" in Croatian means that when he joined actively, when he came. But we may ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can spend much time debating these matters. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We see that different dates are given for your joining, 16th or 18th. Can you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I think that this is a technical mistake. On the 16th, in the morning, I was taken away by the civilian police, and indirectly I was a participant. These instructions were probably issued by the brigade on the 18th, saying that I should go to Krtina-Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say you were taken away on the 16th by the police, you ended up at a place where there were lots of other people gathered, didn't you, at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that known to be a place for Croats to meet for mobilisation purposes?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Croats and Serbs; all who were in Vitez at that time, except for Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So how had it been communicated to Croats and Serbs that they should mobilise at the police station, the Muslims not having that obligation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Probably in their TO command in Stari Vitez. However, I repeat: We were not told. It's not that I received any information from them. They came and picked me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That must be because they had you on a list, mustn't it? What was the list they would have had you on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The defence department, before the war conflict, had a list of all military conscripts, because I did my military service just like Muslims and just like Serbs did. And there were files that were very properly kept. Both sides probably could have had insight into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So were you, in fact, still a reservist on the night of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I was no reservist.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Look at this map --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you look at this map, please, D88/2. Take your time. You may not have seen the map in this form before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the usher will place it over the place so that we can all see it. We can probably focus in on that a bit, I should think. More. Even a bit more, I think, probably. Thank you very much. Can you just -- that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at the television screen, does that have on it the place where you lived and where your building was? I don't want to take too long, but it's helpful just to have the picture, if you can give it to us. This is the yellow building that you've told us about.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The first one by the stadium.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you can't find it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kristo, if you can't identify it on that map, then say so, and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The football stadium Stari Vitez, the building, the first building that is directly there, that is to say, at the entrance point between Stari Vitez and Vitez. The first row of houses in Stari Vitez, the garages, the soccer stadium, and the first yellow building standing here, this way. I don't think it was marked here, because I've lived there since 1992 and I'm sure that I -- 1982, and I'm quite sure that I know where each building is, pretty well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you tell us that from your apartment you saw something of some trench-digging on the soccer field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, not on the soccer field; on both sides of the road that goes through Stari Vitez by the stadium to the bus station, or rather the Vitez Hotel. This is a two-way street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And who did you see digging these trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Which Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Local people from Stari Vitez, Mirsad Izet and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ask them what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why not. It was a matter of concern to you. Why didn't you ask them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I didn't think it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you were a member of the local party, weren't you, the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, only since 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, my mistake, yes. Well, did you draw to the attention of any official that there was this trench digging going on?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. It was common knowledge. It was a matter of concern, and I did comment about it with some people, but I had no right to ask someone personally why he was digging trenches. I felt I did not have the right to ask them because it was next to his house. It was his land, his property. Where did I get the right to ask him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This was an individual person, just one individual or a couple of individuals, is this right, digging trenches at their houses?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're not aware whether this is recorded anywhere in a contemporaneous document?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course by this time, a great deal had happened in Vitez that could have worried Muslims, that would be correct, wouldn't it? Not just what the Serbs were doing.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Things happened that worried Croats too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's just deal with my question first. There were a great deal of things done in the way of taking over the town that could have been disturbing to Muslims. You would accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I can't accept what you say fully, a lot. There were individual incidents that concerned the Muslims but that concerned me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course there had been attacks in nearby Novi Travnik which is only a small distance away in June and in October of 1992, hadn't there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By the HVO against the Muslim interest?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That is not correct. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who do you say was attacking whom on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The Muslims were attacking the Croats. That was the information I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What were they doing that for, did you understand?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, I said, and I repeat, until the last minute of the conflict, I was convinced there would not be an open war between Croats and Muslims. So everything that was done was done by irresponsible individuals. Those were incidents and my colleague, my neighbour -- my colleague at work, who was a Muslim, had a less reason to feel insecure than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: As a politician who was popular among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, because I did not live in Busovaca. We did not have any personal contacts. I don't remember that I ever had the occasion or the honour to sit down in company with such an important gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know that he was associated with the attacks at -- or the fighting at Novi Travnik to put it neutrally in both June and the autumn of 1992? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Why would I know about it when, in 1992, I was engaged in my own business and I was not concerned with politics or the war or the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the Herzegovinians, were you aware of the Bruno Busic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I saw members of that brigade in town, but I did not have contacts with any of them so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can't help us one way or another with when they left, can you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: As far as I can estimate, in early 1993, because from then on, I didn't see them around anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the night of the 15th, you were asked if you were aware of the forthcoming troubles, and I have noticed that you said, "Most people were unaware."

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were those, to your knowledge, who were aware? If most were unaware, it sounds as if some were aware. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, probably those who were in charge of the army and who were in charge of politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did your answer "Most were unaware," reflect the fact that you must have discussed this with other people and discovered that some people had been informed that trouble was coming?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: On the contrary. All the people I talked to said they had known nothing, just as I hadn't known anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. So after these events, despite talking to people, nobody ever told you how it had all happened; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If I were to suggest to you that there were meetings on the 15th in the evening, meetings where there was a plan and where there was disagreement between military and senior representatives of your small town, you've never heard anything of such things; is that your account?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have I got this much of the picture correct: You went back to Stari Vitez or the Mahala, as it's otherwise known, for just three days on the instructions of somebody at the police station; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it may be my mistake for not understanding your evidence. But after your short training at the police station, did you go back to Stari Vitez, the defence line there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I spent three nights there and on that third day, I went to the line in Krtina-Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps you would just be good enough, I don't want to take a lot of time with the map, but if you can help looking at the map and point out where you say you were, that will assist us. Can you look at the map? Does it show where you were? Look at the map, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The other part of the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll have to give you a map with a different scale.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You are indicating a position to the right of Sivrino Selo, and --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And is that where you were immediately after the meeting at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: After, on the third day, I was sent to this line. It's interesting that the place name is not here on this map, and it's bigger than Sivrino Selo. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The first three days, have I still got this right, you were over to the west of the position you've told us in the area of Stari Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's correct. At the Pavlovici line --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you point that out roughly where that was on this map?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. The place where I was on the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that's right on the road going out of Vitez. So you must have seen the truck bomb. Did you see the truck bomb on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Not on that road. Not on that road. I apologise, there is another road. The main road, it's the next road parallel to this, Vitez Stari Vitez, the bus station. It's another road, not on that road, but across the road. I didn't see the truck bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You must have heard about it or you must have heard it.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I heard about it later on, but I wasn't present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For these three days, what were you doing so far as Stari Vitez was concerned, keeping people in?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: There were no people. We were facing the line and I was only on duty. I did not fire a bullet during those three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just help me.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mahala or Stari Vitez contained a number of residents all or most of them Muslim; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, but not all, most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were manning a line. Did that line block the exit for Muslims if they had wanted to come out of their enclave?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: The line on the entrance to the town, that's what I'm trying to say, not the exit. The exit is where the church is in the direction of Travnik. It was the other part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was the line you were on, and you've shown us it roughly on the map, a dividing position with Croats on one side and Muslims on the other?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, there is a road running across. It's a byroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the Muslims were on the one side, if they had tried to pass your line, you would have stopped them, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Probably. Just as they would have stopped us if we had tried to go into Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mahala was a closed off enclave, and you were one of those keeping them prisoner. Why were you doing that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That is not correct. I was on quite another side. My line was surrounded on three sides by Muslims; Sivrino Selo, Sljivcica, Barin Gaj. Why did they expel my people from my village of Poculica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We haven't got to Poculica yet. I'm asking what you did immediately after --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- the fighting broke out. So --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I was carrying out my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who gave you your duty?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I was defending my family. I gave myself my duty, and so did my command or rather whoever was in charge of the overall activity, the overall policy, the overall defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So on the 17th of April you weren't yet a soldier; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't yet have a commander of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't part of the controlling political party, you tell us?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's correct. The ruling --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And yet you would have stopped Muslims from having free access to their town. Why would you have done that, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No one was trying to make them leave the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You must understand my question, Mr. Kristo. You were manning a line that the Muslims would not be allowed to pass, and you were doing it apparently by instinct or by your own judgement. Now, why were you doing that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, because they wouldn't let me pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Muslims from the yellow building, what happened to them when you went to the police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: They were taken away. They were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why were they imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: They were detained primarily because no one could be safe among the Muslims, whether they were soldiers or simple citizens who were welcome. That's one reason. Another reason is that uncontrolled armed groups were moving around and they might have killed them, because they had been expelled from their own homes and they were indignant. They had been expelled by Muslims, like my people from Poculica, my brother, and they might have shot at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So no one could be safe among the Muslims. What was it about the Muslims that made it unsafe to be amongst them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's not correct that they were not safe. If they hadn't been safe, they wouldn't have gone to the elections with us and voted for the same goals and tied flags together and had a common policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm just going to cut you short. I was simply reading back to you part of your answer, "No one could be safe among the Muslims," and I wanted you to tell us why you said that to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's not true that I said that no one could be safe among the Muslims. I say it's not true. It must be a misunderstanding. No one could be safe among the Muslims or among our people, that is, the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Working platoons, until the end of April, were moved about by armed guards taking them under compulsion, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You go on to something about people being used elsewhere. I'm only concerned with the period until the end of April at the moment. Where did you have experience of working platoons between the 16th and the end of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Until the end of April, in Krtina-Mahala, trenches were dug by members of the army, people from the village who were not military able, and 8 or 12 Roma who during the night dug communication trenches, a long Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. trench connecting two trenches, and they were treated humanely and sent back, and no one else did that. But two or three months later I heard from rumours that Muslims had also been brought to some lines but that they had been treated properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not going to respond to those rumours. Just help me with the Romanies. The Romanies were used, was it, after the Muslims had all left? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Not all the Muslims left Vitez. They worked as members of the work platoon, mostly the Muslims that stayed until the end of the war who were in mixed marriages, Mr. Gerim and others. And the Roma insisted when they were going to the line that they should stay together. That was part of their mentality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware of people actually dying when forced to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: When you say "dying," you do mean they were killed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Killed, shot.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. How many do you know about, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I think that one was killed on the line where we were. He was hit by Muslims certainly, because there were no Croats or Serbs on the side the bullet came from. And it can be checked. There are documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was to these positions that Romanies and Muslims were taken to dig trenches; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just two or three questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe we can talk about the last point. Did you have an opportunity on any occasion to see members of work platoons, any work platoons, either from the villages or from the town, being put in positions that were dangerous for them to dig?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: I did not see that on other lines. On our line, we put them in places that were safer than the places we were at. I shared my sandwiches with them. I did not keep the better part of the sandwich for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In those hundred or so days on your line, were any soldiers wounded, colleagues of yours, while digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- I think his name was Ivica. He was a refugee from Zenica, so I cannot recall his last name at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Just two questions about the trenches you talked about for quite a long time. First of all, would you tell me: After you saw the two trenches dug by the Muslims at the edge of Mahala around the road connecting the town, did the Croats then dig trenches in the same place?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Well, not there, because there are no Croats in that part. It's 150 metres from my building, and there were no trenches dug in the town itself at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did Croats dig trenches anywhere around Mahala?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question: My learned friend suggested to you that you Croats were preventing Muslims from leaving Mahala. I will ask you the following: On that -- from that morning when the conflict began, you said your house was shot at?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that was the morning the war started?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And had there not been shooting on that morning, would you have gone to the line facing Mahala or something else?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: As I said, I would have gone to work again, because I had left my calculator there and my bag and other things. I am engaged in business, not military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And no one would have prevented you from going to work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No, no one. That's interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And although considering the place where you lived and the place where you worked, you passed through Mahala every day to go to work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: That's correct, every day. And I had contacts with Muslims. I have even very good friends among the Muslims who went to school with me, played soccer with me, played cards with me, played chess, and so on. That's interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, that was before. But did you still have Muslim colleagues the day before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: Yes. On Thursday, yes. Kadir Hrustic. He walked with me from Princip to Mahala to his house, and then I went on to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did any of the Croats or Muslims tell you there might be a problem the following day?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRISTO
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kristo. That concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. We'll adjourn now. We'll take a slightly shorter break --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I am pleased if I was able to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until 20 past 11.00. We'll take a slightly shorter break to make sure we finish by 1.00. Twenty past 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning Mr. Miketa, thank you for coming here and -- [Microphone not activated] [In English] ... leading question on the personal data, strictly leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please confirm this for me. You reside in Vitez in the area of Kamenjaca, just yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If it's not correct, just say no. You were born on the 3rd June 1943 in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are of Croat ethnic background and you are a Roman Catholic by religion.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are married and you are a father of three.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: More precisely, you have one son and two daughters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Their ages are between 16 and 29. Is it correct what I said, one son, two daughters?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are a history and geography teacher in the elementary school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At this point, you are no longer a principal but you used to be a principal.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: That is correct. I used to be a principal and now I am just a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You graduated from the teacher's college in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, in 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You are a member of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, I have been a member since it was established in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you have any -- do you hold any office?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. I am just a teacher, and this is the only activity I am involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. This concludes my preliminary questions. Now, Mr. Miketa, after the war in Central Bosnia, do you consider yourself responsible for anything that went on there as a person?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Like other people did, I also attempted to live with others and to survive there, and I do not feel responsible for any of the crimes committed there because I was not involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll come back to that at the end. When did you start -- when did you start working in the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: In 1970 or, more precisely, 21 September 1970.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When the JNA aggression against Bosnia started which was supported by the local Bosnian Serbs, did you continue with school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, but because of shelling and because of the air raids of the -- by the JNA, we interrupted it often. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean whenever there was any specific danger, you would interrupt school for several days?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: It was open-ended. We didn't know how long the danger would last, but we would then tell children not to come to school if there was a danger of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: However, the school year went on until when?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, with these frequent interruptions and under difficult circumstances, it continued on until 16 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was the day when the open conflict started between Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. That is the day when the -- that unfortunate conflict between the Muslims and Croats started. And until then, we were able to work in the school with these interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, can you very briefly describe where your school building is?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: The school building is in the centre of Vitez town. Unfortunately, it happened to be situated right at the line of separation of the two warring parties so it was impossible to have classes during that period. On the 16th of April, I learned that it was impossible to access the building because the conflict had just broken out. One colleague, female colleague told me that it was impossible to approach the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, where is the secondary school centre in relation to the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: They are almost adjoining. It is about -- they are about 30 metres apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there is also a small sports stadium adjoining these two structures?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. It is a stadium of the Vitez soccer club, and that was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And if people were shooting from Mahala to -- in the direction of the school or the other way, there was nothing in between?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, there was just a clearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the building often?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, I frequently went to the school which was to complete my work, to put away the documents, because this was a sudden interruption and I found some people in the school building whom I did not know, and this is why I wanted to put those documents away, because it was important for the children or for us. It was -- these were documents relating to the children and so I went to the school as often as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where was the administrative part of your school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: That was in the central section of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was that part open towards Mahala or was it protected?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: The offices were protected for a while, but the classrooms and the cabinets were not protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that from the start of the conflict some people were in the building.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was this the military?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. I did not see those. There were some people on the rooftop who were observing around. I had no access to that part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But those were some units who were on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can I conclude from this that you were unable to identify these people?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I did not know these people. I did not know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you able to say anything about the insignia or any other identification marks?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I never saw any insignia that they were wearing, because I had no contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From that time on, the soldiers were continuously in the building?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, they were there continuously. When I came later on -- and I came on several occasions later -- they were there. But I noticed that they were coming and going. They were coming in shifts. I did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you give us a figure how many people; five, ten, or many more?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I just noticed that these people were observing Mahala, a small number of them. I don't know if there were more of them hidden somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, in the neighbouring secondary school centre, was the situation similar? Were some soldiers also deployed there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that building. I don't know what was in there. I only know about the building where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Earlier, that is, in late 1992 and early 1993, was the school building used as a reception centre for the refugees who were coming to the Vitez area, especially after the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Even before the fall of Jajce the building was used as a reception centre for refugees who were arriving in waves from Kotor Vares, Kljuc, Jajce, and surrounding areas. I, actually, was one of the organisers of these refugees. The organisation was such that we asked locals to bring along some food for the refugees, and I'm quite proud that we were able to help the people who came. And even to date, when I go to my hometown of Jajce, people thank me. They say, "You helped us," and I don't even recognise the person. So that gives me a sense that we've done something good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, what was the ethnic structure of these refugees?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: As I said, they came from Kljuc. Kljuc was predominantly Muslim. Kotor Vares was both Croat and Muslim. Jajce, both Croats and Muslims and even some Serbs. Because I knew some people from Jajce personally, because I myself am from Jajce. So we immediately would accommodate them in various classrooms and we organised food for them, meals. And there was also a team which was in charge of finding accommodation for them in the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate number of refugees who came through this school building over that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I believe it was about 5.000, but I remember when Jajce fell on 30th of October, 1992, this number was approximately around 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean at one time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that number because the accommodations were not right. We did not have enough space for such a number of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the days leading to the conflict of 16 of April, there were no longer any refugees in the school building?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: The refugees had left in late 1992. Because, of course, after October it gets very cold, and we did not have heating in the elementary school in Vitez, so most of the refugees were accommodated either somewhere in the Vitez area or they had moved on. In other words, they were not there anymore at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time when the conflict started, was the school building ever used as a detention centre or a place where people were held captive?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I said that until the 15th of April, children were there and we who worked there. And on the 16th, the military arrived. There was no one else in the building. And as I said, the refugees had left long before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But now let me take you to May 1993. Was anybody placed there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. As I said, nobody was there except for those soldiers, and occasionally some of the school officials would come, mostly looking for information what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please ask the registry to provide document Z882, please. [In English] Would you please put it on the ELMO. There is no Croatian text. This is the original English document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miketa, let me first explain to you what this document is so that I can ask you these questions.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From the heading, we see that this is from the regional centre of Zenica. It's the humanitarian office in Zagreb. It's a UNHCR report. It is a special report of 4 May 1993. It is signed by a certain Mr. Henk Morsink. First, let me ask you this: Have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Second: Do you know the person who signed it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I can't see the bottom of the document, but it is not -- let me see. You said Henk Korsink [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. Henk Morsink.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I never heard of this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, let me take you to the contents of this document. It says that a team is conducting an investigation pursuant to allegations that two Muslim families were being held in the school building. Then it is mentioned that this team first visited the commander of the brigade, Mr. Cerkez, the commander of the Vitez Brigade, in order to be able to make this visit. I am going to skip several paragraphs. And the third paragraph from the bottom, it says that a neighbour directed these people to seek shelter in the school building, that the school principal at that time did accommodate these people. They were not held in the school building against their own will and were treated well. Then on the 3rd of May, another group of HVO soldiers arrived in a red van. They broke the windows and again threatened these families. And in closing it says that the brigade commander knew that the extremists -- that there are extremists around, and that he said that he was looking for them and that he would take care of the safety of these families. In that connection let me ask you this: In those days from the start of the conflict and during the period referred to in this document, early May, during these visits when you went to deal with the administrative matters, did you ask anybody for any permit?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, I was not required to ask anyone for any permit because I was the principal of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you recall in those early days of May that you accommodated any families in the school building?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I hear this for the first time. I pointed that out that the refugees had left in late 199 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, let us not repeat all that.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: After they left and until the conflict, there was nobody in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, let us be perfectly clear on this, do you allow a possibility that this claim that two Muslim families were accommodated in the school building on the 4th of May? Could such an assertion be truthful at all?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: That the school building was under the army control and there was no possibility of families to be there, maybe they were somewhere around there but not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you, as a principal, asked to accommodate anybody there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, and I had no authority there at all at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In addition to the two school buildings, your school building and the secondary school building, is there any other school building in town?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, not in town, but there are outside of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is there a school in Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, there is a school in Dubravica. It is about two kilometres away in the direction of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, in these proceedings it was mentioned several times, but do you know whether -- who was billeted in the Dubravica school in early May?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I don't know this because I was on duty in the school, and I don't know who was billeted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that somebody was billeted there, that somebody had a base there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the adjoining school building, the secondary school centre, was it -- would it have been possible for families to be there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
