utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps the principal of that school could be asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, would you have learned about this, given that you visited the school building on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I certainly would have because when I go from my home to the school, I pass by that other school. And I would have learned, you know, this is a small town. I would have learned something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During the former Yugoslavia, what was the name of your school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: It had -- it had a name, it was called the Brotherhood Unity elementary school and it was not unique, about 150 schools of the former Yugoslavia had that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Why did you change that name immediately after the elections?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: You know, we were very bitter, both the adults and children. We were embittered by the previous system, and especially after the shelling of Vitez, we tried to forget everything that had anything to do with the former system. This is why the name of the school was changed and it was now called the Vitez elementary school. I thought that that name would not bother anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, this decision was taken by the staff?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. This decision was taken by the council of Vitez, of the municipal council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But it was proposed by the staff?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, because they were all very irritated by the name. They said, "Well, if everything else has gone, that should go too," and we decided to propose this to the municipality and they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am being advised that I am going too fast. It is my fault, I am not allowing time to -- between the questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When were you principal of the school, between what dates?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I was the principal between 1991 until actually very recently, until the 1st of this month. So I was principal for eight to nine years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Just one moment, I've got something for the legal officer, could I hand it over. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should just clarify this for the Trial Chamber, a follow up to this question. According to the law, did the principals change every four years?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you were principal for two terms?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, you could be for two or more terms if the school authorities agree with it, if the municipal authorities agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in order to become a principal, you had to have support of your colleagues, of the teachers' council?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were changing the name of the school, did you get any directive, any instruction from the education ministry of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, because at that time, Bosnia-Herzegovina, we could say, did not practically exist. We had -- we were not in touch with Sarajevo. The communications were very poor at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina and there was no coordination with the Ministry of Education let alone other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, let's clarify this too. Let's say from the early summer 1992 and at any time after that, did you, as a school principal, receive any official document from the Ministry of Education in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, I never received any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Because our regional office, the ministerial office was in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you receive any documents from the regional office in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. I had a feeling that we had been completely forgotten, that we were completely forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was the only authority with whom you had any contact?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: For the most part, we had communication with the municipality, that was the only thing, and we had contacts with the Herceg-Bosna community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the period immediately before the war, how many teachers were there in school, and what was their ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: There was a total of 55 teachers on the staff, and the majority were Bosnian Muslims, about 50 per cent; Croats, about 35 per cent; and then the Serbs and Montenegrins.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a school principal, did you or your fellow Croat teachers create a situation in any way that your fellow Muslim colleagues would leave their jobs?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, we continued giving classes. It wasn't regular, but until the 16th of April 1993, we worked, and there were no problems. There were not even any misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, as a school principal, did you at any time in 1992 or early 1993 give the teachers in the school, did you give them any oath of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. loyalties to sign, oath of loyalty to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, we didn't give them any oath of loyalty. It was not necessary to sign any oath of loyalty because they were there in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive such documents and never distribute them around or did you never receive any of those?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I hear for the first time that such documents should have been given out to people. We never received any such instructions or documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As regards the fact the teachers left: Before the open conflict of 16 April, is it a fact that some teachers did leave?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. Even to date I don't understand. The Serb teachers left. They made various excuses. They said that their mothers died or they had to go for treatment, they went to visit family. Somebody said that he had to have a memorial service for his mother, who apparently had died 40 days before. So even to date, I don't know why some of them left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did some Muslims also leave?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. At that time they did not leave, that is, until that real conflict of the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When Muslims left, were did they go?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: For the most part, to Mahala, Zenica, Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the summary, and now I'm referring to paragraph 3.3. In the former Yugoslavia, the language taught -- what was the name of the language that was -- what was the official name of that language that was taught?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: At that time it was called Serbo-Croatian language. But that was not a mother tongue for all of us. That was the official language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time when you changed your name and when Bosnia became a sovereign country, you were not any longer part of Yugoslavia, what did you do about the name of that subject?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: As I said, people were very upset by the aggression of JNA in Yugoslavia. They wanted to cut all ties with the past and they refused to use the texts written in the Serbo-Croatian language. I can say that as we did not have the ministry of education, the schools were somewhat independent, so we did whatever we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what did you call that subject then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Where there was -- where we had opportunities to get textbooks, because we had no contacts with Sarajevo, we changed that -- the municipality, actually, did it, and it was renamed the Croatian language, and that was our mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, will you please help me and the Trial Chamber on this, to clarify this. In everyday use, not in the school, when you say, "Write me something in this language," how would you call this language, when it was -- even before Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: We used "Serbo-Croatian language".

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the official language?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia, when you talked informally, say over dinner, would you use the name "Serbo-Croatian" or "Croat Serbian language"?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What would you use?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: We would say "Croat Serbian" or we would say "Croatian language."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, did the term "Bosnian language" or "Bosniak language" or "Muslim language" exist?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Believe me, we heard of that language for the first time after the war. We had never heard of "Bosniak" or "Bosnian language." As I said, the only language that used to exist was Serbo-Croatian, and later Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, you said that you heard an official -- Bosnian language referred to as official language only after the war. Did you learn that in Sarajevo University there was a chair of Bosnian language which was established only in 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a widely known fact. I even know people who went to study it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to help -- to finish this portion on the language, could the usher please assist me to distribute a new document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked Defence Exhibit D125/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you please review this document, Mr. Miketa. My first question to you is: Have you ever seen this document? That is, did you see this document at the time when it was published?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is this the decision which you mentioned in which the official name of the language has now changed into the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to paragraph 2. Will you please read it and tell me what it means.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: "The parents of students and students may use another term for the language, in which case they are obliged to engage a teacher of the language in question."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is this about? Why did the municipal government add this paragraph to the decision?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Because in addition to the Croatian children, there are Muslim children, there are Romany children and Serbian children, and they could have had classes in their own language if we could find teachers for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did any ethnic community ask that this be respected and that a teacher in their own language be engaged?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, I would like to ask you to take a look at yet another document, please. I think you will be able to tell us something about that. In the meantime, before you receive this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. This document is not having a translation. I did put it to the translator before. I'm waiting for a translation. But I will only ask for the two names out of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D126/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, please take a look at the signature on this document, the name of the person who signed this document. Tell me, please: Do you know the gentleman who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: This is Nuraga Mulahalilovic. He is principal of the school, of the secondary school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Oh, so he was the principal of the other school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You know him very well professionally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: But of course. We often attended meetings of school principals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What is he by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this document now. Tell me, what is it, and what is the purpose of this document? What kind of a document is this?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: This is the kind of certificate that I used to issue as well when I would employ a person, either for a fixed term or for longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this is a document on the basis of which employment is initiated?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. The worker starts to work in accordance with this document and enjoys the same rights as those persons who already work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know Hakija Cengic, the person who was being employed on the basis of this document?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally. He was employed in our school for sometime, and for a long time he was principal in the school in Bila, a school that is not far away from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic was certainly a very competent teacher?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, and he was very knowledgeable in terms of military doctrines, military skills, because he was reserve officer school, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, is this the same person who was head of the Territorial Defence in Vitez before that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. I know that because when a person would leave Vitez, that person would have to get a certificate from the Territorial Defence in order to be able to move to a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when Mr. Hakija Cengic no longer worked for the Territorial Defence he went back to work in a school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: He had been employed in a school before that as well. So it is possible to do it that way. When somebody is appointed to a special job when his term expires then he can go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps we should let others --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel stop overlapping the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the regulation stipulated that a person could go back to his original job?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, that is what happened to me as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, two matters. The first is this, Mr. Kovacic, the interpreters are having difficulty because you are speaking at the same time as the witness. Could you listen out, please. The other point is that this document will not be admitted until such time as there is a translation. It can have that number but it will not be admitted until it's properly translated. And, Mr. Kovacic, please let the witness give the evidence. Have you, in fact, got very much more for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that I could be finished in 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But I'm sorry for that document, Your Honour, I'm really trying to avoid using the documents untranslated but just as example, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, finally, what ethnicity is Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic is a Bosniak, a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three brief questions, just give yes or no answers. Let us save time. You don't have to explain anything additionally. You mentioned this when you spoke about language, anyway, is it correct that after changing the name of the language, you also started changing textbooks?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was the objective for this to avoid textbooks that had been prepared, written, and published in the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: The only reason was to avoid that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So was this actually a situation in which you had to use textbooks where it would say in textbooks related to social sciences that there was brotherhood and unity and equality among all nations, and then one part of that country is conducting aggression against another part of that country?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. That is, as I said, one reason we wanted to break off from the past. That was a initiative taken both by parents and students.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, did you ever receive instructions from someone that you should replace the textbooks that you had been using until then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. I never received any such instructions because I was looking for a possibility to get anything but what we had been using until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where did you manage to obtain some textbooks from, at least some?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: The only thing we could do was to seek them in the Republic of Croatia and that was the only links that existed anyway so I managed to get them in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Another question related to textbooks. After the new sovereign independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was established, were textbooks being published at all? Was a single textbook published in Bosnia after sovereignty?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Until the present day, textbooks are not being published in Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are printed in Slovenia for Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is no possibility now, nor was there any possibility then to have these textbooks actually printed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Miketa, at the outset, I asked you whether you thought that you were responsible for something, for any activities that took place during the course of the war. I would like to ask the registry to have document D42 [as interpreted] placed on the ELMO and in front of the witness, please. [In English] It's wrong in the transcript, it is 40/2. [Interpretation] Mr. Miketa, let me just tell you about this. This document was signed by its author, Mr. Nihad Rebihic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I know Mr. Nihad Rebihic. He was a colleague of mine professionally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you worked for him for a certain period of time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, we never worked in the very same place. One of us worked in the centre and the other one worked in the outskirts, but we worked for the same enterprise, the same school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did he sometimes manage to get to the central school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was this the normal way in which one would work his way up the ladder in the school system?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. It is the opinion of parents and children that was taken into account for one to reach the central school. This was a kind of award.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a teacher and as a person, do you think highly of this man as a person and as a teacher?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, I can hardly say anything about him because we had very few personal contacts. I only saw him at meetings of the central school -- at central school meetings. We did not really have any personal contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This document is called -- it is called the list of persons interesting for reasons of security who are suspects or who are responsible, "List of persons interesting for security reasons suspected of being responsible for or directly connected to the crimes, genocide and ethnic cleansing of Muslims in the area of the Vitez municipality." Tell me, Mr. Miketa, on page number 2, please look at paragraph number 4. Unfortunately this text is in English, but I will help you. This man mentions your name stating that you are a war criminal. Let's check this out. Do you think you are, Mr. Miketa?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I don't know. If I was principal of a school, and if it's a crime to be principal of a school, then I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, let's check some of this out. Are you the father of two sons?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: At the very outset, I said that I have two daughters and a son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this one son of yours, was he a sniper during the war?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: By the way, was he of age during the war?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. Well, he turned 18 sometime during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is mentioned here that you were among the most important people in the HDZ and later in the HVO. What was the highest position you held in the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I was one of the five or three vice-presidents, that is the highest position I held, but in Vitez in the municipal committee. I was one of the vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you vice-presidents have separate areas of work, did you specialise?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: We mainly helped the president in some fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can one say that you were primarily involved in certain fields?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. This is all very general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in the HVO, when the HVO local government was formed, did you hold any position there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, I held no office there. I was only at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have an unofficial position, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know whether it is a special office to help take in refugees which I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, you already mentioned that. Were you engaged in any way in the procurement of weapons for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, no. No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the procurement of weapons for the HVO in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you think there's anything wrong about the fact that you brought in new textbooks, inter alia, from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I think I actually helped both parents and children, so that the children would not waste a school year. This was the only way in which we could obtain books. Why would one not help if one can? Losing a school year is very -- it's very important that children do not lose a school year, especially children attending finishing years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, did you directly take part in the detention of Muslims in concentration camps in the Vitez area, in the arrest, maltreatment, and imprisonment of Muslims in concentration areas in the Vitez area, especially in the settlement of Kolonija?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: First of all, I do not live in the settlement of Kolonija, and I did not participate in such activities. Anybody can confirm that. Arrests? I don't know who was involved in that kind of thing at all. I was in a completely different part of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one question in relation to this, Mr. Miketa. At any point in time after this unfortunate war, did any representative of the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or a Prosecutor, investigator, anybody from this Tribunal, did anybody ask you for an interview as part of an investigation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, nobody talked to me. If anybody came to see me, they only came to talk about school matters, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, did you travel through Bosnia in the meantime, from the end of the war until the present day?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You never moved from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: While I was there, and I would mainly travel between Travnik, where the school centre is, and I also went to visit my family in Jajce, nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did any police stop you anywhere? Did they ask you to show your ID or something like that, your documents?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, no one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now when you travel to The Hague --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- did you require any security measures, you personally?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. No. I'm a free citizen. I don't think that I have jeopardised any person in any way, and I feel free to go to any part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. In conclusion, just one question: Did you know the accused Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know Mario Cerkez. Mario Cerkez was one of my students. He was a good student. And I'm glad to have seen him a bit. I know him. I knew him as a young boy, although later we would not see each other very often once he left school. But I know his family as well. Vitez is a small town. We all know each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything bad about his family?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what about Mario himself?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of him being opposed to any particular ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, of course not, and I know he wouldn't do anything like this. I've known him since a young child.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever notice during all those years in Vitez that he appeared in public as some kind of a prominent figure?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: As I said, when he left school, I hardly ever saw him. I never heard anything bad about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No further questions for you, Mr. Miketa. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions for Mr. Miketa.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was your son a member of the Vitez Brigade in the war?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did he --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Yes, he was a member of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did he join up?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I and all other people in Vitez were in the guards, and he was too. And when he joined up, that I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He became an active member of the Viteska Brigade, did he?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked about this document D40/2, written by Nihad Rebihic and we see dated as early as the 10th of June, 1993. Two points, first of all: You can't point to any particular reason why the author of this document should misreport events about you, can you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I could not mention a reason, but he probably could not get a promotion, and perhaps that is why he was angry with everyone. Could I explain that? He could not get promoted within the school. He always worked at the village school. He never came to the central school. So perhaps that is one of the reasons, and it has nothing to do with me personally. I imagine it could be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you think personal jealousy, as it were, or personal frustration, personal frustration --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe. Maybe that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you just look at the allegations that are made against you, first about your son, about your son being a sniper, and then about being engaged in acquiring weapons for the HVO. Let's just pause at that one. Is there any truth in that, about your acquiring weapons for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: There is no truth in that. I only worked for the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just dwell on that for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have a closed session just for the purpose of identifying a name -- private session, rather.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would like to talk about that man, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us leave it for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just two things I want to ask you. One at the moment. You've told us about making trips to Jajce before the outbreak of the fighting, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. My family lives there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you came back from Jajce, before the outbreak of fighting, from time to time you brought weapons with you, didn't you, and ammunition. Do you remember? Think back.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: That's what you say, not I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking of you and suggesting to you and that you distributed the ammunition and the weapons amongst fellow Croats. Think back, please. Take your time. It's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: There is nothing to think about. I went to Jajce to visit my parents, and the last time I was there was during the bloodiest fighting, when the Serbs were conducting an aggression against Jajce. That's when I was there. And no weapons could be brought from there, nor were there any weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the document we were looking at, D40/2. It says that this man said of you that you were one of the main advocates of HZ HB, Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in Vitez. We've heard of your position as deputy chairman or whatever it was. You were an advocate, weren't you, of the community of Herceg-Bosna? You believed in it.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I was one of the deputy chairmen of the municipal board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You believed in Herceg-Bosna. You advocated it.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, I should explain now because it seems that you do not know what the situation was so I should talk about it. When the aggression started, and we had no contacts with Sarajevo, with Bosnia-Herzegovina, when there was nothing, we had to find a way. We had to find someone to protect us. And that was the only reason. It was for our survival.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Herceg-Bosna was a Croat-based body, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It was mostly for the defence of the people who lived in that area, all the ethnic groups, to protect ourselves from aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In November 1991 when it was formed, what aggression were you facing then, please, Mr. Miketa?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: In 1991, that was when we hoped, after the attack on Croatia or rather we expected an attack after the attack on Croatia, and it actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've spoken, you see, of your judgement of Mr. Cerkez. Now, you are an educated man. Is the reality this, that people of all sorts of earlier behavioural patterns were driven in the course of 1992 and 1993 to become partial to one side or another of an ethnic divide. That's what happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Please. Well, I know there was chaos at that time, total chaos, and I cannot say who was partial and who was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All sorts of things drove people to take ethnic sides where they might not have done formerly. The parade in 1992 at the soccer stadium, did you go to that?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. No. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The propaganda was advanced on behalf of Herceg-Bosna, wasn't it, on the television?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I think at that time -- well, I don't remember whether we had any television then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the document. It says here that you were responsible for the introduction of the Croatian curriculum and for abolition of the curriculum and textbooks of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I was not responsible. I simply transmitted the proposals of the teachers and the pupils, the parents of the pupils to the municipality and that was it. I transmitted the proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll have to look at that document in just a second. But would you accept this, that you ordered the teachers in your school that students, Muslim and Croat, were to be taught only the Croatian language and not the Bosnian language, and that you did that in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I will say again I did not order. Everybody accepted this voluntarily, and you made a mistake. There was no Bosniak language at the time. As I have already said, this happened only after the war in 1994 when they established a chair in Sarajevo, and it was from then on that the Bosniak language began to be spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What would you say to the suggestion of the evidence that you directed your teachers to teach only Croatian music and songs at the same time, September of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I can tell you that we did not know that then. We studied what we knew from before. We did not even change the music.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could I have a very short private session, if that's acceptable to the Court, and the exhibit that I have been touching on is 1771.2, paragraph 3 of it, and it was a summary that was incorporated on this occasion into the evidence for want of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the person who we are not going to name publicly who I have just spoken of and whose evidence has been given in this case, can you think of any reason why that person might misrecord events as against you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, I don't know her very well because she worked in the school for a very short time. I don't know why she would have anything against me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the man called Munib Kajmovic who has been a witness in this case, open session, page 3845, do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I don't know him personally but I know where he worked. He worked in the secondary school if you want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he was a member, did you know this, of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I don't know that. I am not interested in personal things of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see he's told us, Mr. Miketa, and he was at a school, he's told us that the Vitez Muslims agreed that the language to be used in schools should be the Bosnian language at the end of 1992. You tell us that there was, as it were, no knowledge of the Bosnian language until 1994. Think back, please. Isn't it right that people were using the term "the Bosnian language," and understanding it, well before this conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: You obviously don't understand something. So the Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You must not personalise things, we are in a Court. You've said so far --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Your evidence has been that the Bosnian language did not come in until after the war. Now that's your evidence.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and I stand by that. Because if we say "Bosnian", that belongs to me too because I too live in Bosnia and so do Serbs and Roma and others. So we all speak Bosnian. But when you say "Bosniak", that's something different because I also have the right to call my language Bosnian as does everybody who lives in Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, that language does not actually exist. You can talk about the Bosniak language, and that's probably what they want.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your exhibit or the exhibit that you have introduced, we'll have a look at it if necessary, D125/2, said this: "Parents of students and students may use another term for the language, in which case they are obliged to engage a teacher of the language in question." Does that mean obliged to engage a teacher at their own expense?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. Today, there is still a law in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the Federation, that every pupil has the right to his or her language if there is a sufficient number of pupils in a class. And in my school if, for example, there were 30 or 24 pupils in the 6th form, I was obliged to find teachers who would teach them in their language. That was what was intended, and not that parents would employ the teacher but the school and the municipality would, and this law is still in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we can see from the document, perhaps it should just go on the ELMO once more so the Chamber can see it if they haven't got it, 125/2, we can see that this is a Herceg-Bosna order dated the 19th of November, 1992, an HVO order or decision and it reflects only the HVO government's adoption at a session of itself on the 19th of November of a decision. It then says, "In conformity with the government's decision." Which government would that be, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: As far as I know, until the outbreak of the conflict on the 16th of April, 1993, in the municipality, in the government, there were also people of other ethnic groups and the assemblymen of both Bosniak and Croat and Serb ethnicity who were in the municipality at the time in the government issued this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm right then, that this is an HVO decision, isn't it? All of which comes from a non --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: This is a decision by the municipal authorities, the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was non-elected and basically a Croat body; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Not just Croat. There were Muslims in the government then as well, and the SDA, and the HDZ and the SDP. Everybody who was in the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Ivan Santic who appears to have signed this is your friend, I think, the president of the HVO, sometimes so-called Ivica Santic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was the president of the local government at the time --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: He was then the head at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And who lives where now, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: In Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And he's alive and well and you've seen him recently?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: That's right, I have. And he was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A quick look -- he was here, was he? I see. A quick look at 653.1. When was he here, by the way? Mr. Miketa, when was he here?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't know when he was, but you know he was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This document, if we can just look it. Put the English on the ELMO, please. This is dated the 14th of April of 1993. And if we look just at the bottom of the document, it's an order from Valenta, and it says that schools will cease working -- this is dated the 14th of April -- will cease working until Monday, the 19th of April. Was that the reason there were no children in your school at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: When do you mean? When the attack started?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When the fighting started, yes. Is this the reason your school was empty of pupils?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, that happened in the morning, and there were no classes, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, we were attacked on the 16th of April, early in the morning, so of course there were no children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, this is an order dated the 14th of April. I thought your evidence was that children weren't very much in school at that time in any event. And this is an order that would cover the week of the 14th to the 19th of April, signed by Valenta. It goes to the presidents of various municipalities, including Vitez. Was this the order that led to there being no pupils in your school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, I have already said that children went to school up until the 16th, so the 15th was the last time they were there. There were regular classes. And then there was a sudden interruption in classes on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to deal now, because we're running short of time, I want to deal now with the night of the 15th, 16th. Your house is near to or adjacent to Stari Vitez or the Mahala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, not right next to it, but nearby. Not adjacent, but close. As the crow flies --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: -- about a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In that area there is a Muslim house occupied by a family Hrustic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. No, there's no family like that there. In that part there is no family of that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, after these events unfolded on the 16th, you must have appreciated that a number of houses quite near to you were completely destroyed, with loss of life following the destruction; correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: You are completely wrong. No houses were destroyed where I lived, no houses, nor were any of our neighbours injured. Others were, our people, but no houses were destroyed where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that -- well, your area was no doubt a Croat area; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. No. No. My next-door neighbour is a Bosniak, a Muslim, and the one next to him too. On the right-hand side there are mostly Croats, but it's a mixed settlement where I live, a mixed neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know these people by name? No, I shan't bother with that, for want of time. On the morning of the 16th --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th there was, in fact, a heavy attack on Stari Vitez, on the Mahala, wasn't there, by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No? And --

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: There was no attack. We were attacked from Mahala by -- and from the neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was the apparent purpose of the people in the Mahala attacking you? Explain it to us. What could they possibly achieve?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, probably with support from outside, from other areas, they did have a purpose. I don't know what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. You've never been able to work it out, even since 1993, Mr. Miketa?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know a man called Ivka Mlakic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Is it a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. A woman, Ivka Mlakic. My mistake.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... by the name of Mlakic in your area?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, there's a whole village of people with Mlakic as their last name, a whole neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in that morning, the 16th of April, a rocket launcher was used from gardens of the people called Mlakic, in your presence, and it was fired at the Mahala, wasn't it, with devastating results?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: My house faces Mahala, and behind the Mahala, if you look at the map, you will see there is a big hill, and then there is the village of Mlakici. So I couldn't see what was behind the hill. And on the 16th I couldn't even raise my head because of the shooting from Mahala. I had a lot of problems, but those are my personal problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. There's only one detail that I think the Chamber might be assisted by. It relates to the Morsink document. I haven't got time to go into it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, this: You've been asked questions about evidence that's been given about a family taking refuge in a school, and this would be in May of 1993. Are you really saying that your knowledge of your school is so comprehensive that you're excluding the possibility of families being kept in that school for their safekeeping, or is it possible that they were and you simply didn't get to know about it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: There is no reason for me not to know, because I came to the school often. And the only place I didn't have access to was the roof, where there were observers, where there were military men. Everything else was accessible to me. So I can state responsibly that from the end of 1992, when it grew cold, there was no one in the school at all, because all the refugees were accommodated in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We know that the Dubravica school to the east was used for prisoners, but in the centre of Vitez how many other schools were there? Just yours, or was it your school and one other school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: There was also a secondary school in Vitez, and it is some 30 metres away from the school where I work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Santic tell you what happened on the night of the 15th, 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I have not had contacts with Santic, because I live in a village, and we did not have any contact for a long time, because I simply couldn't go to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: So there was nothing that he could have told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As the vice-president of the political party of which he was the president, my last question to you: Are you telling the Chamber that even when you were able to meet him, you never asked from him and never learnt from him what happened on that terrible night? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: I learnt that there had been atrocities, which I condemned, terrible atrocities, and we all feel that those responsible must be brought to justice. But I did not find out any details. I only learned details later on from the media, from newspapers, from the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just shortly. I don't think that there is too much. Your Honour, unfortunately, because of technical reasons, and I never believed that it is challenged, but I will introduce the evidence and I will now just use the witness to make explanations so the document will have a certain value. Otherwise I have to call another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miketa, I have in my hands a letter from the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo, dated the 21st of December, 1992, and they are answering an inquiry by my investigator and they say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. It's 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And since the founding of the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo from 1950, there has been a chair for southern Slavonic languages. Up to 1994 there were two chairs: the chair for the modern Serbo-Croatian language, with general linguistics, and the chair of historical disciplines. And from 1994 on, the chair for modern Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian language, with linguistics, and the chair of historical disciplines. Mr. Miketa, you, as a person in this profession, did you know this before I read you this letter?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, I never heard of this. I know only that in 1994, a chair for the Bosniak language was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may reserve the number for that and we will of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, when it's translated. May we have a number for it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D127/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One more point. I will ask you to answer very briefly so that we don't waste time. Who is the aggressor on Bosnia? Who was the aggressor in 1992, which force, which army?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, everybody who lives there knows that it was the JNA. That was the JNA with -- well, with the support of the Serbs of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The textbooks you had at that time were published by the same state whose instrument, whose army, the JNA was; is that true yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the same time, did the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina either before or after independence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just draw your attention to, amongst other consequences of cutting my cross-examination, I didn't ask any questions on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. We've heard enough about this. I should add that counsel is right, no questions in cross-examination were asked about textbooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps not directly but, of course, I will not ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivica Santic has been mentioned but my colleague has reminded me in the cross-examination, Mr. Kajmovic was mentioned, yes?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know him. I only know that he works in the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether, at any time, Mr. Ivica Santic, whom you were asked about, was the president of the HDZ party?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, Ivica was never the president of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was his post in 1992-1993?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: He was the mayor of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How did he become the mayor?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, the leading parties in Vitez agreed by ballot that he was able to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was that on the basis of the election?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was there any doubt that he was elected democratically to be the mayor?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. He was a very honest and able man to do the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Miketa, as a responsible person in the school, did you and your teachers on the 16th of April 1993 tell the children not to come to school on the following day?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. It happened so suddenly, who could have told them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were any instructions issued to the children earlier about how they should behave as regards coming to school if there was danger?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Well, even during peace time, in the former system, we always had to bear in mind that if there was any danger of some kind, we should know where the children should -- what routes they should use to get out of the school where they could take shelter. We knew that even in the '80s. Later there was no other instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were shown an order, so to say, issued by Valenta about stopping school. First of all, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, never. This is the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did anyone at that time tell you there was such an order?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No, I never heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And thirdly, had you received this document from Valenta, was he competent to tell you whether there would be classes or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: No. We were not responsible to Valenta, we were responsible to people in the education department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And one more question, a very simple one. Your trips to Jajce have been mentioned. At the time you said you went to Jajce to visit your parents, what units were fighting against whom?

utterances.speaker: ANTO MIKETA
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I was there during the fiercest fighting when the air raids on Jajce started. That's when I was there. And the people were unarmed and they were opposing the aggression of the JNA and the Serbian army, the Serbs, and Muslims and Bosniaks and Croats were fighting side by side on the same lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Miketa, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Miketa, if you would like to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may be short, extremely short. I think that we ought to inform you about -- that we have certain objections. It is lately that Office of Prosecution is more and more, through the cross-examination, is using the documents which we -- which are not introduced earlier, which are for us entirely new documents, which are not discovered in any form to the Defence. And in addition to that, we suspect on some sources used that also are intelligence documents of the Bosnian authorities, we cannot approach so we cannot check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When something concrete rises, we've heard what you say but, Mr. Kovacic, the easiest way to deal with it is in a concrete situation. And if you have an objection to a particular question, then of course you must make it as you did this morning. We hear your general objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, we will do that. But merely for practical reasons in order not to interrupt the cross, if I may suggest also a proposal that I think that there is obligation that the Prosecution should transmit such documents to the Defence. Then we could be prepared for such documents. Then we could see the other questions, of course, from the document. There is no need to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have a limit of time that I can sit now and we have been sitting for nearly two hours, I think. We hear this. Perhaps you would raise it again if you wish to on Monday. The Prosecution hear it and they can consider the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. If I just may add if the Prosecution could give us as soon as possible the translations of the statement of the witness we just received today, because there is not too much use if we are having it only in English. Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry for taking up time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two short matters. First, we would also ask for Croatian translations of the documents that were delivered to us today be made available to our client for reasons which I am sure are obvious to the Court. Second, I'd just like to remind the Court that -- Krizanac will be the first witness on Monday, one of the affidavits witnesses that we had committed to the Court to come to testify. Naturally, our direct examination will be extremely terse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the topic of translations, I was thinking that at some stage Monday we may discuss it. No translation in the B/C/S yet, and always a security problem in obtaining one. A possibility would be providing tapes as we've done on earlier occasions. That would need, I think, either undertakings or orders of a protective nature by the Court. Can I find out over the weekend how long the first alternative would take. I think it's already been bespoken, I hope it has, and then we can consider the second as a quick alternative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We'll adjourn now. Half past nine Monday morning.
